lesson.title: Learn, don’t copy
lesson.subtitle: Use AI as a tutor, and be open about it

video.title: Learn, don’t copy
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — maths teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: Honest use and your school’s rules

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds two perfect homework sheets side by side. Behind her, two test papers: one full of working, one almost blank. She looks from one to the other.
scenes.animation: The two homework sheets slide in side by side, each with a row of ticks; the test papers flip over one by one.
scenes.narration: Two of my students both handed in perfect homework. In the test, one solved every question. The other couldn’t even start. So what was different?

scenes.visual: Paper-grey title card: the Darsi mark, the course name, the lesson title and the yellow AI track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how to use AI so that you’re the one who learns.

scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: a girl works through the steps in her exercise book, asks a chatbot one question when stuck, then carries on writing. Right: a boy pastes questions into a chatbot and copies the replies.
scenes.animation: Left: pencil moves steadily, one question bubble pops up. Right: copy and paste icons flash quickly.
scenes.narration: The difference was who did the thinking. One worked through the steps herself, and asked a chatbot to explain when she got stuck. The other pasted the questions in and copied the answers. Same homework, very different practice.

scenes.visual: A loop of three arrows: try, get it wrong, fix it, around a small brain that glows brighter with each turn. Then an exam hall: rows of desks, no phones.
scenes.animation: The loop turns twice and the glow grows; cut to the exam hall.
scenes.narration: Your brain learns by trying, getting it wrong and fixing it. That struggle is the learning. If AI does the trying for you, you skip the part that teaches. And in the exam hall, there’s no chatbot: only what you practised.

scenes.visual: A dusty school pitch. A coach explains with a whistle, sets out cones for drills, and watches a player dribble. In the corner, someone sits on the bench watching the coach jog, not moving at all.
scenes.animation: Cones drop into place (150 ms each); the player weaves through them.
scenes.narration: Think of a football coach. A good coach explains, sets drills and watches you play. But nobody ever got fitter by watching the coach run.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI chip. Two columns of request cards: on the left, requests that help you learn; on the right, requests that do the work for you.
scenes.animation: Cards drop into each column as they are said (250 ms apart).
scenes.on_screen_text: Honest use: AI helps you learn
scenes.narration: Honest use means AI helps you learn, and you’re open about how. Asking it to explain, to quiz you or to check your work is learning. Asking it to do the work, then handing that in as yours, is copying, even if you change a few words.

scenes.visual: A school notice board with two task sheets: one stamped ‘No AI’, one ‘AI for ideas and checking’. A student raises a hand to ask. In the corner, an app’s sign-up screen shows an age check.
scenes.animation: The stamps land one after the other (150 ms); the hand goes up.
scenes.narration: Rules differ. One teacher says no AI for a task; another allows it for ideas or checking. Your school’s rules decide, so ask when you’re not sure. And many AI tools have a minimum age, often thirteen, with a parent’s permission under eighteen.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds up three request cards like a hand of playing cards, one eyebrow raised. The cards drop in below her.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Which of these is an honest way to use AI for homework?

scenes.visual: The ‘Quiz me’ card gets a check badge. The student answers question after question; the chatbot marks one wrong and explains it.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); answers tick in one by one.
scenes.on_screen_text: A tutor, not a copy machine
scenes.narration: “Quiz me on chapter three.” You still answer every question yourself, and the AI shows you what you missed. That’s AI as a tutor, not a copy machine.

scenes.visual: The bottom of a homework sheet with one handwritten line about how AI was used. Beside it, a folder of rough notes and drafts.
scenes.animation: The line writes itself (1 s); the drafts fan out of the folder.
scenes.narration: When you hand work in, say how you used AI. One line is enough: “I used a chatbot to explain fractions, then did the questions myself.” Keep your notes and drafts too. They show your thinking, and tools that claim to spot AI writing are often wrong.

scenes.visual: A phone shows the lab: a six-by-six school yard with walls and puddles, a robot in the bottom corner and its charger in the far corner. After practice, arrows fill the squares and a chart of steps per trip falls.
scenes.animation: The robot wanders, then takes a short path; the chart line drops (1.5 s).
scenes.narration: In the app, a robot must cross a school yard to reach its charger. Nobody shows it the way. It learns from its own tries: a reward at the charger, a penalty in puddles. Press Practise, and watch its trips get shorter.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds a homework sheet with an empty line at the bottom. Answer cards appear beside him.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. You used AI to explain a topic, then did the work yourself. What should you do when you hand it in?

scenes.visual: The ‘Say how you used AI’ card gets the check badge, then four summary lines tick in under ‘Remember’.
scenes.animation: Lines appear one by one, 250 ms apart.
scenes.on_screen_text: Say how · Own tries · Tutor, not copier
scenes.narration: Say how you used AI: one honest line is enough. Remember: like the robot, you learn from your own tries. Use AI to explain, to quiz you and to check your work, never to do it for you. And your school’s rules decide.

scenes.visual: A student at home with a notebook and a phone. The chatbot asks a question; the student writes an answer, gets one wrong, reads the explanation and nods. End card: the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Question and answer bubbles alternate; a tick and a cross pop; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: pick one topic, and if you’re allowed to use AI, make it your tutor. Ask it to quiz you, and answer every question yourself. Then ask it to explain your mistakes. It’s harder than copying, and that’s exactly why it works.

checkpoints.prompt: Which of these is an honest way to use AI for homework?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — you still answer every question yourself, and the AI shows you what you missed.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — if the AI writes the essay or the answers, it did the practice, not you. “Quiz me” keeps the thinking yours.

checkpoints.prompt: You used AI to explain a topic, then did the work yourself. What should you do when you hand it in?

options.text: Hide it: nobody needs to know

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — one honest line about how you used AI is enough, and your school’s rules may ask for it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — even honest help is worth mentioning. One line about how you used AI keeps you in the clear.
